title: Client Feed Validation, First Impressions Count
description: Enterprise client onboarding through CSV feed validation: canonical mapping, reject-warn-autocorrect classification, idempotent re-ingestion, and the follow-up email that builds trust while surfacing problems.

sources.title: Take-Home Assignment: Client Positions Feed Onboarding

lines.text: New enterprise client sends their first positions export. Twenty-five rows. Nine problems hide inside.
Missing dates. Negative quantities. Duplicates. Unknown fund codes.
Reject the whole file?
Rejecting the file rejects the relationship. This is the first technical exchange.
Goal: find problems before the client does, communicate them in a way that builds confidence.
Dana from Meridian Capital sent her first CSV export. This is the first technical exchange.
One bad experience here kills the relationship before it starts.
Exactly. The validator finds problems. The email communicates them professionally. Both matter equally.

sections.title: What blocks, what warns, what auto-corrects?

lines.text: Project ingests CSV positions and maps to a canonical internal model. Every issue gets severity classification.
Reject: record cannot be trusted. Missing identifier, unparseable quantity, unknown fund code with no resolution.
Warn: probably fine but flag it. Unusual date format that parses, zero quantity on closed position.
Auto-correct: safe deterministic fix. Whitespace trim, date normalization, currency symbol strip.
Who decides which is which? You do, and defend it.
That decision IS the skill being tested.
Assignment has three parts: build validation service, write client email, document AI usage.
Timebox: two hours total. Complete smaller solution beats ambitious fragment.
AI assistants explicitly permitted and expected. They evaluate how you use them.
Canonical position model normalizes field names, types, units. Client sends position_date; internal calls it as_of_date.
Idempotency: re-running on same file produces no duplicates.
Deterministic content hash per record becomes dedup key.
Conflicting re-delivery: same logical position arrives changed. Needs deliberate handling, not silent overwrite.
Options: latest-wins by timestamp, manual queue, versioned records. Choose and defend.
Canonical position model normalizes everything into consistent types and units.
Client column position_date maps to internal as_of_date. Client sends dates as month day year format; internal stores ISO format.
Quantity might arrive as text with commas: 1,500.5. Parser strips formatting, converts to decimal.
Currency symbols stripped. Negative quantities flagged depending on context.
Idempotency uses SHA-256 hash of canonicalized record values concatenated in fixed order.
Same logical position produces same hash regardless of column order or whitespace differences in source CSV.
What about legitimate updates where a position value changes between exports?
Hash includes all fields. Changed quantity means different hash, detected as conflicting re-delivery.
Resolution policy needed: latest-wins by as-of date, manual queue, or versioned records preserving history.
Prototype chooses latest-wins with audit log. Simpler and defensible for initial onboarding.
Input: sample CSV from Meridian Capital, fictional wealth platform.
Validator reads, maps columns, applies type coercion and validation rules.
Output: structured report with accepted, rejected, warned, auto-corrected counts plus row-level detail.
Sample report ships with code so grader sees results immediately.
Part two: write follow-up email to Dana, integration lead, technical but not engineer, two hundred to four hundred words.
Structure: what works first, then blockers prioritized, then clarifying questions, then next steps both sides.
Why does tone matter in technical exercise? Forward-deployed engineering is client-facing.
The email IS part of the product.
Sample feed walkthrough with actual problems found.
Row three: fund_code ABC123 exists nowhere in reference data. Reject: cannot verify fund exists.
Row seven: quantity negative fifteen shares. Could be a correction or a data entry error.
Classification depends on business rules. Prototype warns and flags for review rather than rejecting outright.
Row twelve: date formatted as December thirty-first twenty-twenty-four instead of standard format.
Parser recognizes natural language date and auto-corrects to ISO. Logs transformation.
Rows eighteen and nineteen identical except one has trailing whitespace in fund name. Hash deduplicates correctly.
Validation report summarizes: sixteen clean, five warnings, three rejects, four auto-corrections across multiple rows.
Email to Dana opens: thanks for sending the first export. Good news: most records map cleanly.
Then prioritizes blockers: three rows could not be processed due to missing fund references.
Asks clarifying questions: should negative quantities represent corrections or errors? What is the authoritative fund code list?
Proposes next steps: Dana confirms fund codes, we adjust mapping, schedule next export.
Out of twenty-five rows, sixteen accept cleanly, five warn, three reject, several fields auto-correct.
Re-ingesting identical file produces identical result: zero new records, zero duplicates.
Hash comparison milliseconds for thousands of rows. Millions need batch processing and indexed hash column.
Prototype proves correctness small-scale first.
Processing performance on sample scale.
Twenty-five rows parse and validate in under fifty milliseconds on a laptop.
SHA-256 hashing per record: microseconds. Negligible overhead.
At enterprise scale, millions of rows need batch processing and database indexing on hash column.
But prototype proves correctness at small scale first. Premature optimization hides logic bugs.
CSV arrives. Column mapping translates headers. Type coercion normalizes dates and numbers.
Validation rules classify issues. Content hash enables idempotent re-runs. Conflicts surface deliberately.
Report outputs summary and detail. Email communicates findings professionally.
Complete flow once more.
CSV arrives. Column mapping translates headers to canonical names. Type coercion normalizes dates and numbers.
Validation rules classify issues as reject, warn, or auto-correct. Content hash enables idempotent deduplication.
Report outputs summary counts and row-level detail. Follow-up email communicates findings professionally with clear next steps.
Client changes column order next export. Sudden mass rejection. Fix flexible matching with clear error.
Encoding issues break parsing. Fix try multiple encodings, log success.
Duplicates arrive across different files, not just re-runs. Composite key including source metadata.
Pending: export frequency? Authoritative source system? Known upstream quality issues? SLA for corrections? Who owns data quality on their side?
Additional edge cases worth anticipating.
CSV encoding shifts from UTF-8 to Latin-1 between exports because client changed their export tool.
Signal: sudden decode errors on characters that worked last week. Fix try multiple encodings, log which succeeded.
Column renamed from fund_code to security_identifier with no notice.
Signal: mass rejection on previously clean column. Fix fuzzy header matching with warning when uncertain.
Duplicate positions arrive across different files representing genuine separate holdings.
Signal: hash collision on logically distinct positions sharing all attribute values. Fix composite key including source file metadata.
Pending questions: export frequency? Authoritative source system? Known upstream issues? Data quality ownership on client side?
Re-run same file, get byte-identical output?
Every rejected row has machine-readable reason code?
Would your follow-up email make client trust you more or less?
Fourth: does your validator distinguish I found a problem from I do not know how to interpret this?
Fifth: if the client fixes all issues and resends, does your system accept the corrected file without duplicating anything?
Self-test: valid quantity but fund code exists nowhere in reference data. Reject, warn, or something else?
Next time: supply chain scheduling where FIFO meets capacity constraints and material availability.
What about incremental feeds where each export contains only changes since the last one?
Different ingestion model requiring delta detection. Worth designing but beyond initial scope.
